guide.title: Columbia, Connecticut: A Schoolhouse That Seeded Dartmouth
guide.intro: Columbia began as the North Society of Lebanon, known to settlers as "Lebanon Crank," and was incorporated as its own town in May 1804, taking the patriotic name Columbia after the national personification of the United States. In 1754, the Rev. Eleazar Wheelock founded Moor's Charity School here to educate Native American students; the surviving 1755 schoolhouse still stands on land donated by Joshua Moor. Wheelock moved the school to Hanover, New Hampshire in 1769-1770 under a royal charter, where it became Dartmouth College — the last college chartered in colonial America before the Revolution. Mohegan minister Samson Occom, who raised some 12,000 pounds in England for the school, protested that Wheelock diverted the money to found Dartmouth instead. Columbia Lake is man-made, created in 1865 when a Willimantic linen company flooded local meadowland for millpower, and the town's 19th-century economy ran on water-powered lumber, grist and paper mills.

sections.heading: Moor's school and the road to Dartmouth
sections.body: The Rev. Eleazar Wheelock founded Moor's Charity School in 1754 to give Native American students a classical Christian education; the surviving schoolhouse, built in 1755, still stands on Columbia Green, its land and building donated by Joshua Moor. About 67 Native students attended between 1750 and 1768 before Wheelock moved the school to Hanover, New Hampshire in 1769-1770 under a royal charter, where it became Dartmouth College — the last college chartered in colonial America before the Revolution. Mohegan minister Samson Occom, who had raised roughly 12,000 pounds in England for the school, protested that Wheelock diverted the money to found Dartmouth instead. Columbia Green's other Revolutionary connection: officers of General Rochambeau's French army were quartered at the Landmark Inn here while planning the march from Newport, Rhode Island to Yorktown, Virginia. The green, with 43 contributing buildings, was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1990.

sections.heading: Getting there
sections.body: Columbia has no passenger rail station and no interstate of its own. Route 66 is the main east-west approach, running from I-91/I-691 in Meriden through Marlborough into Columbia, where it meets Route 87 and then US Route 6 at the west end of the Willimantic bypass. Route 87 (Trumbull Highway) is a two-lane rural road running north from Route 32 in Franklin through Lebanon and Columbia center, skirting the north shore of Columbia Lake before crossing into Andover. US Route 6 clips the town's northern side, reached from I-84 via I-384, which ends at US 6/US 44 in Bolton Notch. There is no CTrail Hartford Line station anywhere in eastern Connecticut; the nearest stop with both Hartford Line and Amtrak service is Hartford Union Station, about 25 miles west, and New London, about 30 miles southeast, is the nearest Amtrak/Shore Line East stop. The Windham Region Transit District serves Columbia as a Dial-A-Ride member town (860-456-2223); its fixed routes run on corridors outside Columbia.

sections.heading: Where to eat
sections.body: Columbia's dining clusters along Routes 66 and 6: The Main Moose is a roadside stand for burgers, hot dogs and ice cream, reopened in July 2026 under new ownership; Motta's Bakery is the town's full-service Italian-American bakery; Thunderbird Cafe is a weekday breakfast-and-lunch counter; and Faith Cafe, inside Crossroads Fitness Center, serves nutrient-dense food and gluten-free baked goods. No hotel, motel, inn or bed-and-breakfast could be verified in Columbia itself; the nearest confirmed option is The Inn on Storrs, roughly 10-12 miles north in Mansfield Center.

faq.question: How do I get to Columbia?
faq.answer: By car — Route 66 is the main east-west approach from I-91/I-691 in Meriden, meeting Route 87 and US Route 6 in town. There is no passenger rail station in Columbia or anywhere in eastern Connecticut; the nearest Hartford Line/Amtrak stop is Hartford Union Station, about 25 miles west.

faq.question: What is Moor's Charity School's connection to Dartmouth College?
faq.answer: The Rev. Eleazar Wheelock founded Moor's Charity School in Columbia in 1754 to educate Native American students. In 1769-1770 he moved the school to Hanover, New Hampshire under a royal charter, where it became Dartmouth College — the last college chartered in colonial America before the Revolution. The 1755 schoolhouse still stands on Columbia Green.

faq.question: Is Columbia Lake natural?
faq.answer: No — it is man-made, created in 1865 when the American Linen Company of Willimantic flooded local meadowland to secure waterpower for its mills. The watershed later reverted to town ownership.

faq.question: What trails pass through Columbia?
faq.answer: The Air Line State Park Trail crosses Route 87 on the town's south side, and the Hop River State Park Trail runs along Columbia's northern border, both on former railroad beds managed by Connecticut DEEP.

faq.question: Is there a hotel in Columbia?
faq.answer: No hotel, motel, inn or bed-and-breakfast could be verified in Columbia itself. The nearest confirmed option is The Inn on Storrs, roughly 10-12 miles north in Mansfield Center.

places.name: Moor's Indian Charity School Museum
places.address: Columbia Green, at the junction of Routes 87 and 66, Columbia, CT 06237
places.summary: The 1755 schoolhouse where the Rev. Eleazar Wheelock educated Native American students before moving the school to New Hampshire, where it became Dartmouth College. Town-owned with a permanent exhibit on education in Columbia; rarely open, so call the town (860-228-0110) before visiting.
places.history: Built in 1755 on land donated by Joshua Moor; a 1969 plaque calls it the seeding ground of Dartmouth College.

places.name: Columbia Green Historic District
places.address: Town green and northwest along Route 87 at the Route 66 junction, Columbia, CT 06237
places.summary: Listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1990, with 43 contributing buildings including the Congregational Church, Town Hall, the c. 1736 Eleazar Wheelock House, the Indian Charity School, the Landmark Inn and a Victorian Revival gazebo. Summer concerts are held on the green.
places.history: Rochambeau's officers were quartered at the Landmark Inn while planning the 1781 march from Newport to Yorktown.

places.name: Columbia Recreation Park and Town Beach
places.summary: The town's swimming beach on Columbia Lake, with lifeguards on chair 10:30 a.m.-6 p.m. in season, a boat launch monitored by marine patrol, boat and kayak moorings, and rentable pavilions. Season beach passes sold by the Recreation Department.

places.name: Air Line State Park Trail (Columbia section)
places.address: Crosses Route 87 in Columbia, CT 06237 (southern side of town)
places.summary: A 54.9-mile rail-trail on the old Air Line Railroad bed running through Columbia, with hard-packed stone dust, pavement, gravel and dirt sections. Route 87 in Columbia is a listed access point on the trail's south section.

photos.title: Air Line State Park Trail, Columbia
photos.description: The Air Line State Park Trail inside Columbia town limits.
photos.author: John Phelan

places.name: Hop River State Park Trail (Columbia section)
places.address: Northern border of Columbia, CT 06237, along the Hop River
places.summary: A 20.8-mile rail-trail running from Manchester east to the Air Line State Park Trail in Windham, passing along Columbia's northern border. Used for hiking, biking, horseback riding and cross-country skiing.

places.name: Heartstone Farm & Winery
places.summary: A family-run, 56-acre farm winery with an indoor tasting room and a patio overlooking the vineyard, pouring wines hand-crafted from grapes grown on the property. Tasting room open Tuesday and Friday 12:30-6 p.m., Saturday and Sunday noon-6 p.m.

places.name: The Main Moose
places.summary: A roadside stand with outdoor seating, reopened in July 2026 under new ownership, serving burgers, hot dogs, fried seafood, lobster rolls, Hershey's ice cream and Hosmer Mountain Soda. Open daily; ice cream service runs later than the grill.

places.name: Motta's Bakery
places.summary: Columbia's full-service Italian-American bakery: breads, pastries, cupcakes, cookies and novelty and wedding cakes, plus pizza on fresh-baked crusts, grinders and calzones. Open Monday-Thursday and Saturday 8 a.m.-5 p.m., Friday to 5:30 p.m., closed Sunday.

places.name: Thunderbird Cafe
places.summary: A weekday breakfast-and-lunch counter serving full breakfast until 11 a.m., then sandwiches, wraps and burgers with daily specials, including lobster and clam chowder on Fridays. Open Monday-Friday 7:30 a.m.-2 p.m.

places.name: Faith Cafe
places.summary: A small cafe inside Crossroads Fitness Center focused on nutrient-dense food developed with nutritionists, with gluten-free baked goods. Open Monday-Friday 8:30 a.m.-2 p.m.

links.note: Andover borders Columbia to the southeast; Route 87 crosses from one town into the other.
The Hop River State Park Trail runs through both Columbia and Coventry on its way to Windham.
The Air Line and Hop River trails both connect Columbia to Windham.
Route 66 links Columbia to Hebron on its way from Marlborough.
